title: User Datagram Protocol

hero.subtitle: The simplest transport protocol — connectionless, fast, and minimal overhead

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The User Datagram Protocol (UDP) provides a simple, connectionless transport service for applications that need to send datagrams without the overhead of connection setup, reliability guarantees, or flow control.

UDP is one of the two original transport protocols of the Internet protocol suite, alongside TCP. Where TCP provides reliability, UDP provides simplicity and speed.

UDP adds only a thin layer on top of IP: source and destination port numbers for multiplexing, a length field, and an optional checksum. The entire header is just 8 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The User Datagram Protocol (UDP) is a simple transport service for sending datagrams without connection setup, delivery guarantees or flow control. It adds only source and destination port numbers, a length and an optional checksum on top of IP. The whole header is 8 bytes.

sections.title: Protocol Format
sections.content: The UDP header is four 16-bit fields, eight octets in all, followed by the data octets. The RFC draws it as four 8-bit columns; the diagram below shows the same layout as a 32-bit-wide grid.
sections.plainLanguage: The UDP header has four 16-bit fields, eight bytes in all: source port, destination port, length and checksum. The data follows the header directly.

sections.title: Fields
sections.content:
Each field in the UDP header serves a specific purpose:

Source Port (16 bits)
An optional field. When used, it indicates the port of the sending process and may be assumed to be the reply port. If not used, a value of zero is inserted.
Destination Port (16 bits)
The port within the destination host to which the datagram is addressed. This field is required and identifies the receiving application.
Length (16 bits)
The total length of the UDP datagram (header + data) in octets. The minimum value is 8 (header only, no data). The maximum is 65,535 bytes.
Checksum (16 bits)
Covers a pseudo-header (source IP, destination IP, protocol, UDP length), the UDP header, and the data. Optional in IPv4 (zero if not computed), mandatory in IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The ports identify the sending and receiving programs. The source port is optional and is zero if unused. The length covers header plus data, with a minimum of 8. The checksum covers the header, data and a pseudo-header of IP details. It is optional in IPv4 and mandatory in IPv6.

sections.title: Usage
sections.content:
UDP is the right transport choice when applications value speed and simplicity over guaranteed delivery:

Applications using UDP must handle their own reliability if needed (e.g., DNS retransmits queries, QUIC builds reliability on top of UDP).
sections.plainLanguage: UDP suits applications that value speed and simplicity over guaranteed delivery. Unlike TCP, it has no connection setup, no retransmission, no ordering guarantee and no flow control. Applications that need reliability must provide it themselves, as DNS does by retransmitting queries.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content:
Many of the Internet's most important protocols rely on UDP as their transport:

53DNS — Domain Name System queries and responses
67/68DHCP — Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
123NTP — Network Time Protocol
161SNMP — Simple Network Management Protocol
443QUIC — Modern transport for HTTP/3
5353mDNS — Multicast DNS (zero-config)

The rise of QUIC (RFC 9000) has given UDP new prominence. QUIC builds a reliable, multiplexed transport on top of UDP, enabling HTTP/3 and demonstrating that UDP serves as an excellent foundation for innovation.
sections.plainLanguage: Many core protocols use UDP, including DNS (port 53), DHCP (67/68), NTP (123), SNMP (161) and mDNS (5353). QUIC, which carries HTTP/3, also runs on UDP and builds its own reliable transport on top of it.

references.text: Postel, J., "Transmission Control Protocol", RFC 793, September 1981.

subtitle: The simplest transport protocol: connectionless, fast, and minimal overhead

plainLanguage.summary: UDP sends individual messages between programs on different hosts, using port numbers to identify them. It has no connection setup and gives no delivery, ordering or loss notification. This keeps it fast and light, with only an 8-byte header.

how big is a udp header
what port numbers does udp use

tldr.problem: Some applications just want to send a short message to another program without setting up a connection or waiting for acknowledgments.
tldr.mechanism: UDP puts an 8-byte header (source port, destination port, length, checksum) in front of the data and hands the datagram to IP, which marks it as protocol 17.
tldr.outcome: Delivery, ordering and duplicate protection are not guaranteed, so applications that need them use TCP or add their own checks on top.

today: UDP is still everywhere. DNS queries, DHCP, NTP and many streaming and gaming protocols run over it. QUIC, the transport under HTTP/3, is built on top of UDP so that it can add its own reliability and encryption without waiting for operating systems to change TCP. One later change: the checksum is optional over IPv4, as this RFC says, but it is required over IPv6 (RFC 8200).

messages.label: UDP datagram
messages.note: The sender fills in ports, length and checksum. There is no connection setup.

messages.label: UDP datagram
messages.note: IP hands it to UDP, which passes it to the program on the destination port. If it is lost or duplicated, UDP does not notice or retry.

fields.name: Source Port
fields.desc: Optional. When meaningful, the port of the sending process, and the port a reply should be addressed to absent other information. If not used, zero is inserted.

fields.name: Destination Port
fields.desc: Has a meaning within the context of a particular internet destination address.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in octets of this user datagram including the header and the data. The minimum value is 8.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of a pseudo header, the UDP header and the data, padded with zero octets if needed. All zeros transmitted means no checksum was generated.
